title: When a Beatle Hijacks Your Monologue: Paul McCartney’s Surprise SNL Cameo with Will Ferrell
summary:
Will Ferrell’s return to host Saturday Night Live’s season finale was supposed to be his moment. Instead, it became a masterclass in celebrity hijinks, thanks to a legendary Beatle and a lookalike drummer.

The chaos began seconds into Ferrell’s monologue when Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith—long noted as Ferrell’s doppelgänger—strode onstage pretending to be the host. “I’m thrilled to be back here hosting Saturday Night Live. Thrilled!” Smith announced, resurrecting a bit that dates back over a decade to a drum-off on Jimmy Fallon’s show. Ferrell soon stormed out, scolding the crowd for applauding: “Don’t clap for him. He’s a bad guy.”

But the real twist came when Ferrell, attempting a reset, opened the floor to audience questions. The first hand belonged to Paul McCartney. The former Beatle ambled up, basking in a roar of applause, and promptly turned the tables. “You know what? I think you’re Chad Smith,” McCartney deadpanned, before rattling off his own songwriting credits—including “Penny Lane,” which Ferrell had conspicuously omitted. Then came the command: “Get your butt behind that drum set.”

The bit was absurd, heartwarming, and perfectly SNL. Smith later reappeared as the actual drummer for McCartney’s three-song set, which included “Band on the Run” and “Coming Up.” The cameo underscored McCartney’s playful side and Ferrell’s willingness to be upstaged. For a show built on surprise, it was a reminder that even the biggest stars can’t resist a good lookalike joke—especially when a Beatle is the punchline.
why_it_matters: The skit illustrates how comedy and music can merge into viral moments that define pop culture, reminding you that even legendary figures stay relevant by embracing humour, which shapes how celebrities connect with your generation.

background_read: Saturday Night Live (SNL) is a long-running NBC sketch-comedy show, on air since 1975, famous for surprise celebrity appearances and biting political humour.
Will Ferrell was a cast member from 1995 to 2002, creating unforgettable characters like Ron Burgundy, and returning to host is a major event in comedy circles.
Paul McCartney, one of the two surviving members of the Beatles—the most influential band in pop history—has made several memorable SNL appearances over the decades, often mixing music with skits.

The long-running joke about drummer Chad Smith (of the Red Hot Chili Peppers) and Will Ferrell being lookalikes originated in a 2014 drum-off on Jimmy Fallon’s late-night show, turning their resemblance into a pop-culture meme.
McCartney’s playful interruption fits a tradition of musicians crashing monologues to create viral moments, reminding audiences that even legends enjoy absurd humour.

perspectives.description: Viewers celebrated McCartney’s playful cameo as a reminder that live TV can produce genuine, unscripted joy, and that even the most famous musicians don’t take themselves too seriously.
Some might argue the bit upstaged Ferrell’s hosting moment, turning his monologue into a sideshow for McCartney—a pattern where legacy stars overshadow newer comedy talent.
The episode highlights SNL’s long-standing formula of surprise drop-ins, which keeps the show in headlines but can make the writing feel reliant on guest firepower over original sketches.

As viral moments like this spread instantly online, SNL may double down on celebrity walk-ons, potentially shifting how new comedians get discovered—a trend that could shape the comedy landscape you grow up watching.
